verses.1:1: And the word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai, saying,
verses.1:2: "Rise, go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim against it, because their evil has come up before Me."
verses.1:3: Yet Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD; he went down to Joppa and found a ship heading to Tarshish, paid its fare, and went down into it to go with them to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.
verses.1:4: But the LORD hurled a great wind onto the sea, and a great storm arose on the sea, and the ship was on the verge of breaking apart.
verses.1:5: Then the sailors were afraid, and each man cried out to his god, and they hurled the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten the load on them. Jonah, however, had gone down into the recesses of the vessel, lain down, and fallen into a deep sleep.
verses.1:6: So the captain approached him and said to him, "What is the matter with you, fast asleep? Rise, call to your god! Perhaps God will think of us, so that we do not perish."
verses.1:7: And they said, each to his companion, "Come, let us cast lots so that we may know on whose account this calamity is upon us." They cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.
verses.1:8: So they said to him, "Please tell us on whose account this calamity is upon us. What is your work, and where are you coming from? What is your land, and from what people are you?"
verses.1:9: And he said to them, "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry ground."
verses.1:10: Then the men feared with great fear and said to him, "What is this you have done?" For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, since he had told them.
verses.1:11: So they said to him, "What should we do to you so that the sea may grow calm for us?" For the sea was growing ever more stormy.
verses.1:12: And he said to them, "Lift me up and hurl me into the sea, and the sea will grow calm for you, for I know that on my account this great storm is upon you."
verses.1:13: But the men rowed hard to turn back to the dry ground, yet they could not, for the sea was growing ever more stormy against them.
verses.1:14: Then they called to the LORD and said, "Please, LORD, do not let us perish for the life of this man, and do not lay innocent blood upon us; for You, LORD, have done just as You desired."
verses.1:15: So they lifted Jonah up and hurled him into the sea, and the sea ceased its fury.
verses.1:16: Then the men feared the LORD with great fear, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and vowed vows.
verses.2:1: Now the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the fish's belly for three days and three nights.
verses.2:2: Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the fish's belly.
verses.2:3: He said, "From my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered me. From the belly of Sheol I cried for help; You heard my voice.
verses.2:4: And You cast me into the depths, into the heart of the seas, and the current encircled me; all Your breakers and Your waves passed over me.
verses.2:5: And I said, 'I have been driven out from before Your eyes,' yet I will look once more toward Your holy temple.
verses.2:6: Waters hemmed me in to my very life, the deep encircled me, seaweed was bound around my head.
verses.2:7: To the bases of the mountains I went down; the earth—its bars were behind me forever. Yet from the pit You brought up my life, LORD my God.
verses.2:8: When my soul grew faint within me, it was the LORD I remembered, and my prayer came to You, to Your holy temple.
verses.2:9: Those who pay heed to worthless vanities abandon their steadfast love.
verses.2:10: But as for me, with a voice of thanksgiving I will sacrifice to You; what I have vowed I will fulfill. Salvation is the LORD's!"
verses.2:11: Then the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto the dry ground.
verses.3:1: And the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time, saying,
verses.3:2: "Rise, go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim to it the proclamation that I am speaking to you."
verses.3:3: Jonah rose and went to Nineveh in accordance with the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was a great city to God, a three-day walk.
verses.3:4: Jonah began to enter the city, a one-day walk, and he proclaimed and said, "Forty more days, and Nineveh will be overturned!"
verses.3:5: And the people of Nineveh believed in God; they proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from their greatest to their least.
verses.3:6: And the word reached the king of Nineveh, and he rose from his throne, took off his mantle from himself, covered himself in sackcloth, and sat on the ashes.
verses.3:7: And he had it cried out and announced in Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying, "Man and beast, herd and flock—let them not taste anything; let them not graze, and let them not drink water.
verses.3:8: Rather, let man and beast alike be covered in sackcloth, and let them call to God fervently; let each one turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in their hands.
verses.3:9: Who knows whether God will turn and relent, and turn back from His burning anger, so that we do not perish."
verses.3:10: And God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil way; so God relented concerning the calamity that He had spoken of doing to them, and He did not do it.
verses.4:1: But it was a great displeasure to Jonah, and he burned with anger.
verses.4:2: He prayed to the LORD and said, "Please, LORD, was this not my word while I was still on my own soil? For this reason I acted beforehand to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that You are a God who is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and great in faithful love, and relenting over the calamity.
verses.4:3: So now, LORD, please take my life from me, for my death is better than my life."
verses.4:4: And the LORD said, "Are you right to be angry?"
verses.4:5: Then Jonah went out from the city and sat east of the city; there he made himself a booth, and he sat beneath it in the shade until he saw what would happen in the city.
verses.4:6: Now the LORD God appointed a plant, and it came up above Jonah to be shade over his head, to rescue him from his misery. And Jonah rejoiced over the plant with great joy.
verses.4:7: But God appointed a worm as dawn came up on the next day, and it struck the plant so that it dried up.
verses.4:8: And as the sun rose, God appointed a stifling east wind, and the sun struck down on Jonah's head so that he grew faint. He asked for himself to die and said, "My death is better than my life."
verses.4:9: Then God said to Jonah, "Are you right to be angry over the plant?" And he said, "I am right to be angry, to the point of death."
verses.4:10: And the LORD said, "You had pity on the plant, over which you did not toil and which you did not make grow, which came to be in a single night and perished in a single night.
verses.4:11: And should I not have pity on Nineveh, the great city, where there are more than one hundred twenty thousand people who do not discern between their right hand and their left, and much livestock?"

notes.1:4: Literally "and the ship thought to be broken" (Piel of chashav plus Niphal infinitive of shavar), a vivid personification meaning it was on the verge of breaking apart.
notes.1:5: Hebrew sefinah ("vessel") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, distinct from oniyyah ("ship") in verses 3-5, and probably denotes a decked craft with a lower hold.
notes.1:6: Hebrew yit'ashet (Hithpael of ashat, occurring only here in Biblical Hebrew) relates to Aramaic ashat ("think, plan") and means "take thought for" or "show concern for." Hebrew ha-Elohim could also be rendered "that god," referring back to "your god."
notes.1:7: Hebrew beshellemi ("on whose account") uses the shorter relative prefix she- (matched by beshelli, "on my account," in v. 12), equivalent to the fuller ba'asher lemi in v. 8.
notes.2:1: In the Masoretic Hebrew versification followed here, 2:1-11 corresponds to 1:17-2:10 in most English Bibles.
notes.2:2: Hebrew uses the feminine form ha-dagah here in place of the masculine ha-dag ("the fish") in 2:1 and 2:11, referring to the same great fish.
notes.2:5: The Masoretic Text reads akh ("yet" or "surely") followed by the auxiliary idiom osif lehabbit (Hiphil of yasaf plus Hiphil infinitive of nabat, "I will look once more"), expressing renewed hope in contrast to Jonah's despair.
notes.2:9: Hebrew meshamerim (the sole Piel occurrence of shamar in the Hebrew Bible) paired with havlei-shav (literally "vanities of emptiness," a poetic idiom for false gods) contrasts idol worship with "their steadfast love" (chasdam), which can mean either their own loyalty or the faithful love God extends to them.
notes.3:3: Hebrew ir-gedolah le-Elohim (literally "a great city to God") is a Hebrew superlative idiom meaning "an exceedingly great city," while also hinting at Nineveh's importance to God.
notes.3:4: Hebrew nehpakhet (Niphal participle of hafakh, "be overturned") conveys imminent judgment like the overthrow of Sodom (Gen 19:25), yet the verb can also mean "be turned around" or "transformed," creating an ironic double meaning.
notes.3:7: Hebrew ta'am ("decree") reflects an Aramaic official usage (cf. Ezra 6:14) and creates a wordplay with the verb yit'amu ("taste," from the same root ta'am) later in the verse.
notes.3:10: Hebrew repeats the same root ra'ah both for Nineveh's "evil" way and for the "calamity" God had spoken of bringing, highlighting the reversal of judgment upon their repentance.
notes.4:4: Hebrew haheitev (interrogative prefix + Hiphil infinitive absolute of y-t-b, "do well") can mean either "Are you right to be angry?" or adverbially "Are you deeply angry?"; the same construction recurs in 4:9.
notes.4:6: The noun qiqayon occurs only in Jonah 4 and is of uncertain botanical identity, commonly identified with the fast-growing castor-oil plant. The verb wayya'al can be parsed as either Qal ("and it came up") or Hiphil ("and He caused it to come up") of the root alah.
notes.4:8: Hebrew charishit is a hapax legomenon modifying the feminine noun ruach ("wind"). Commonly linked to the root ch-r-sh ("be silent/still"), it denotes an oppressive, stifling heat, while ancient versions render it "scorching."
notes.4:10: Literally "which was a son of a night and as a son of a night perished," an idiomatic expression for something arising and perishing within a single night.
notes.4:11: Hebrew introduces this closing clause without an interrogative particle, forming an unmarked rhetorical question (literally "and I, I shall not have pity...?"). The phrase "more than 120,000" is literally "more than twelve myriads" (twelve ten-thousands).
